articles.title: How to check a claim when sources are scarce
articles.description: A small, repeatable method for sorting evidence from uncertainty.
articles.rights: Original Evercraft demonstration text. Broad redistribution rights have not been approved.

sections.heading: Begin with the exact claim
paragraphs: Write the claim as one sentence. Identify what could be checked: a date, a number, an image, an institution, or a quotation. A vague statement cannot be tested until it becomes specific.
Separate what you know firsthand from what you heard or inferred. Confidence should follow evidence, not the number of times a claim appears.

sections.heading: Follow the trail
paragraphs: Ask where the claim originated, who first recorded it, when it was published, and whether a primary document is available. A screenshot without context is a lead, not verification.
Look for independent confirmation. Multiple copies of the same original report do not represent multiple independent sources.

sections.heading: Name uncertainty plainly
paragraphs: Use clear labels: confirmed, supported but incomplete, disputed, or unknown. If a source cannot be opened, say it is unavailable rather than interpreting silence as a fact.
Record publication dates. In a disrupted information environment, even accurate information may be outdated by the time it reaches you.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence portable
paragraphs: When rights allow, retain an offline copy of the source, a citation, the date accessed, and a note about what it did and did not prove.
This guide is educational, not an automated fact-checking service.

articles.title: Build a small offline reading shelf
articles.description: Practical ways to retain useful knowledge before a connection drops.
articles.rights: Original Evercraft demonstration text. Broad redistribution rights have not been approved.

sections.heading: Choose what matters
paragraphs: Prioritize reference material that remains valuable without live updates, such as language learning, basic scientific explanations, and public-domain educational texts.
Do not rely on offline pages for information that must be current, including emergency orders, active conflict routes, or medical instructions.

sections.heading: Save for reliability
paragraphs: Use openly licensed or public-domain collections where possible. Keep files in familiar formats, with descriptive names, and test opening them while disconnected.
Carry multiple copies only where appropriate and safe. A downloaded file may be discoverable by anyone with access to the device.

sections.heading: Check what you kept
paragraphs: For each item, record title, publisher, version or access date, and permission status. A file checksum can detect accidental change but does not establish that the original publisher was trustworthy.
Practice a real offline test: turn off Wi-Fi and cellular data, open the file, and confirm text remains readable.

articles.title: What to do when the internet becomes unreliable
articles.description: A clear distinction between degraded service, isolation, and safe local access.
articles.rights: Original Evercraft demonstration text. Broad redistribution rights have not been approved.

sections.heading: Understand the failure
paragraphs: A site not loading can be caused by device trouble, service outage, filtering, or a wider network shutdown. One symptom does not prove censorship.
Check whether trusted contacts on different networks observe the same problem, when doing so is safe. Never expose another person's location or identity to confirm a hypothesis.

sections.heading: Continue carefully
paragraphs: Offline educational collections and previously saved files remain useful without a connection. Local sharing works only when compatible devices and authorized connectivity exist.
Do not assume a consumer tool conceals identity, traffic metadata, or device contents. Each transport and jurisdiction introduces its own risks.

sections.heading: Keep expectations honest
paragraphs: A locally saved document is not an encrypted message. A cached site is not a communications network. No technology can guarantee connectivity during a deliberate blackout.
For high-risk environments, seek current advice from qualified digital-safety organizations before deploying new tools.

articles.title: A safer approach to private reading
articles.description: What offline storage protects, and what it cannot protect.
articles.rights: Original Evercraft demonstration text. Broad redistribution rights have not been approved.

sections.heading: Start with the device
paragraphs: Your browsing experience can leave local traces, including downloads, bookmarks, browser cache, or operating-system histories. An offline copy reduces ongoing network requests but does not make the copy invisible.
Consider whether a shared or confiscated device presents a risk before saving sensitive material. Seek expert guidance if a specific threat is present.

sections.heading: Know what Passage does today
paragraphs: This prototype does not require an account or add analytics trackers. Its local bookmarks are stored in your browser. Downloaded files are standard text or HTML, not encrypted storage.
A device or network operator may still observe access to the hosted page. Passage does not promise anonymous browsing, evasion of monitoring, or confidential distribution.

sections.heading: Use established safety guidance
paragraphs: Keep software updated when possible, understand where backups live, and avoid sharing personally identifying information unnecessarily.
Choose a security strategy based on an actual threat model rather than relying on a tool's marketing.

articles.title: Share knowledge without losing its source
articles.description: A simple chain of attribution, permission, context, and corrections.
articles.rights: Original Evercraft demonstration text. Broad redistribution rights have not been approved.

sections.heading: Identify the author and the rights
paragraphs: An article being publicly visible does not automatically grant permission to republish it. Prefer permission, public-domain material, or an explicit license that covers your intended use.
Keep an attribution record with the creator, publisher, title, URL, and license or permission evidence.

sections.heading: Preserve context
paragraphs: Keep the publication date and indicate whether a copy was shortened, translated, or adapted. If you cannot validate a claim, do not call it verified.
Distinguish integrity from truth: an unchanged file can still contain incorrect information. Source reliability needs independent editorial judgment.

sections.heading: Make corrections possible
paragraphs: Give every edition a date. Mark superseded material and keep a transparent correction history where safe and appropriate.
Passage's sample library is only a design and technical demonstration. Automated third-party ingestion, rights certification, and independent source verification are not active.
